privacy.principle: Security first. The app collects no personal or health data about volunteers or victims.
rules: No accounts, no login, no analytics, no network calls after install.
Tallies store counts only (no names, ages, conditions, or individual locations), kept on-device and cleared by the user.
Manual forms that collect names or medical details (Treatment Area Record, Personnel Check-In) are referenced, not reproduced as data-entry screens.
Where the manual says to label or record a name (e.g., amputated tissue, 3-11; removed jewelry, 3-10), do that on paper. The app does not record it.

sections.title: Safety First
sections.summary: Rescuer safety is always the number one priority. Personal and family safety come before any team response.

items.text: First responsibility: personal and family safety. Respond as a team only after these are secured.
Stay within the limits of your training.
Rescuer safety is the number one concern. Ask first: "Is it safe for CERT volunteers to attempt the rescue?"
Work in the buddy system. Never fight a fire alone.
Goal: do the greatest good for the greatest number.
Each CERT member takes direction from only one person.
Helmet / hard hat
Goggles (protective eyewear)
N95 mask
Gloves: leather work gloves and non-latex exam gloves
Sturdy shoes or boots
Long-sleeved shirt and long pants
Reflective vest
For rescue work: kneepads, coveralls, thick-soled boots are also recommended

warnings.text: CERT safety equipment is generally NOT fire-resistant PPE.
A dust mask will not filter out all harmful materials. If chemical or biological agents are suspected, evacuate upwind and notify professional responders.

review.text: PPE lists differ across the manual (1-25, 1-31, and 6-12, which says "dust mask"). This list combines 1-25 and 1-31.

topics.title: Should we attempt rescue? (by damage level)
topics.summary: Classify the structure, then follow the matching action. If unsure between moderate and heavy, assume HEAVY.

decision.question: What is the degree of structural damage?

indicators.text: Superficial cracks or breaks in wall surface (e.g., fallen or cracked plaster)

action.text: YES. Locate; assess; treat airway, major bleeding, and low body temperature; continue size-up; document.

indicators.text: Many visible cracks or breaks in wall surface

action.text: YES, but quick and safe removals only. Limit onsite care to checking breathing, stopping major bleeding, maintaining body temperature. Evacuate survivors, warn others, minimize number of rescuers and time inside.
NO. Do not enter under any circumstances. Tape or mark the area as heavy damage, warn people to stay away, inform the CERT TL immediately if people are known to be inside.

warnings.text: When in doubt between moderate and heavy, assume heavy damage.
If a building is creaking or "groaning," it is unstable. Do not enter.
CERT volunteers have no legal authority to stop someone from entering an area. You can only warn them and inform the TL.

topics.title: Search & rescue safety rules
topics.summary: The most frequent causes of rescuer deaths are disorientation and secondary collapse.

items.text: Use a buddy system.
Be alert for hazards: power lines, natural gas leaks, hazardous materials, sharp objects.
Never search an area where water is rising.
Use safety equipment (gloves, helmet, dust mask, kneepads, coveralls, thick-soled boots).
Have backup teams to rotate, prevent fatigue, and help if a team gets into trouble. Drink fluids and eat.
Know your limitations: drink, eat, relax, rest.
Never enter an unstable structure.

warnings.text: Breathing dust is the primary cause of rescuer problems after working in a structural collapse.

items.text: Assess the situation: type of event; is air quality or the structure compromised?
Decide to stay or change location. If not in immediate danger, stay and get more information. If officials say evacuate, LEAVE.
Seek clean air; protect breathing passages (cloth or mask, leave the building, or shelter in place in a sealed internal room).
Protect yourself from debris. If trapped: protect your airway, bang on an object or blow a whistle. Yell only as a last resort.
Remove contaminants: remove contaminated clothing, then wash with soap and water from head toward feet.
Practice good hygiene: clean drinking water and sanitation.

sections.title: Team, Size-up & ICS
sections.summary: How CERTs mobilize, size up a scene, organize under ICS, and document.

topics.title: Mobilization (on activation)

steps.text: Secure personal and family safety first.
If your SOP calls for self-activation, go to the pre-designated staging area with your disaster supplies.
On the way, make damage assessments (Damage Assessment Form) for the TL.
First CERT member at the staging area becomes the initial Team Leader (TL); leadership may pass as others arrive.
TL locates the Command Post (staging area or a safer/better location).
Sign in with the scribe (Personnel Resources Check-In), noting skills and preferred assignments.
Receive assignment; keep communication with the TL so resources aren't overextended.

notes: Volunteers in a heavily impacted location should send runners to staging areas for help (Intro p.3).
topics.localProtocol: Activation method, staging area locations, and leadership are set by your sponsoring agency's SOPs.

topics.title: 9-step CERT size-up
topics.summary: Size-up is continual. Use it in any emergency situation.

steps.text: Gather facts. What happened? How many people appear involved? What is the current situation?
Assess and communicate the damage. What happened, what is happening now, how bad can it get?
Consider probabilities. What is likely to happen? What could happen through cascading events?
Assess your own situation. Are you in immediate danger? Trained for this? Have the equipment?
Establish priorities. Are lives at risk? Can you help? Life safety is the first priority.
Make decisions based on Steps 1-5 and your priorities.
Develop a plan of action. Simple plans may be verbal; complex plans should be written.
Take action. Document deviations and status changes.
Evaluate progress at intervals; adjust. (May require going back to gather more facts.)

items.text: Step 1 Time: Does time of day or week affect response?
Step 1 Weather: Does weather affect your safety? The situation?
Step 1 Construction: What type(s) of structure and construction are involved?
Step 1 Occupancy: Occupied? How many likely affected? Special considerations (children, elderly, pets, access and functional needs)?
Step 1 Hazards: Hazardous materials evident? Other hazards?
Step 2: Survey all sides. Is the danger beyond CERT capability? Have facts and initial damage been communicated?
Step 3: Potentially life-threatening hazards? High potential for more disaster activity?
Step 4: What equipment and other resources are available? Can CERT safely attempt response? If not, do not attempt.
Step 5: Any more pressing needs now?
Step 6: Where will resources do the most good while keeping an adequate margin of safety?
Step 7: Determine how personnel and resources should be used.
Step 8: Put the plan into effect.
Step 9: Continually size up for changes in scope, safety risks, resources. Adjust.
The TL reports to the first fire or law enforcement official at the location and takes direction from that person until relieved.
The TL stays in the Command Post. If the TL must leave, TL responsibility is delegated to someone in the Command Post.

tables.title: CERT ICS functions

Fire suppression, medical operations, search and rescue

Communications; food and medical support to team; manages supplies and facilities; ensures adequate personnel, supplies, equipment
Formal ICS function; CERTs have very limited involvement, if any
Formal ICS function; generally not used by CERTs

items.text: Span of control: optimum 5 rescuers per supervisor; acceptable 2 to 7.
Operations teams: 1 to 5 people.
One person serves as runner to the Command Post.
Two people "buddy up" for immediate needs.
Search & rescue teams: at least 4 people. A safety team stays outside the search area; at least 2 conduct the search.
Every unit has an identified leader who supervises, accounts for members, and reports up.

review.text: Page 2-5 says operations teams are 1-5 people, and also that search & rescue teams need at least 4. Both are shown.

topics.title: Media inquiries

steps.text: Refer all media inquiries to the CERT TL.
TL refers them to the sponsoring organization's Public Information Officer (PIO).
If authorized to speak: wait until it won't delay the team's work; set a briefing area; release only accurate, approved information; respect victims' privacy; you need not answer every question.

topics.localProtocol: Your sponsoring agency's PIO decides who speaks to media.

topics.title: Documentation: write it down
topics.summary: The most important thing is to write down what happened. Forms or plain paper both work. Every team or location needs a scribe.

items.text: Command Post documents: incident locations, access routes, identified hazards, support locations (staging, medical treatment area, other areas per Local Protocols).
Give documentation to the first professional responders on scene.

tables.title: CERT standard forms

Staging scribe signs in volunteers: who, when arrived, when assigned, special skills
Command Post; the most important tool for tracking overall situation status
TL gives instructions; team logs actions and reports new damage info; returned on check-in
Treatment area personnel record survivors entering, condition, status
Messages between levels: assignment complete, resources needed, special info, status update

notes: Blank forms appear on manual pages 2-27 to 2-35. The app should link to or describe them, not collect their personal or health fields (see privacy).

sections.title: Triage (START)
sections.summary: START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment), from the program's triage unit. Use it when there are more injured than rescuers. Check RPM, "30-2-Can Do": Respirations over or under 30 per minute, Perfusion over or under 2 seconds, Mental status can or cannot follow simple commands.

topics.title: START triage decision
topics.summary: Work through RPM for each survivor. Failing any one test means Immediate. Everyone gets a tag.

decision.question: Step 1, Airway: is the survivor breathing?
detail: At arm's distance, shake the survivor and shout (T-17).
Position the airway, then look, listen and feel for breathing (T-17).

next.question: Step 1, Respirations: is the breathing rate more or less than 30 per minute?
detail: Abnormally rapid breathing (above 30 per minute) indicates shock (T-17).

action.text: Tag IMMEDIATE ("I", red). Treat for shock. All survivors tagged Immediate get airway control, bleeding control, and treatment for shock (T-18). Everyone gets a tag (T-18).

next.question: Step 2, Perfusion: after the blanch test, does normal color return in more or less than 2 seconds?
detail: Visually check for obvious signs of bleeding. Take immediate action to control severe bleeding (T-17).
Blanch test: press the nailbed base or fleshy fingertip until it turns white, release, and time how long normal color takes to return (T-14, T-17).
The blanch test is not valid for children. Use mental status as the main indicator for children (T-14).

action.text: Tag IMMEDIATE ("I", red). Treat for shock. All survivors tagged Immediate get airway control, bleeding control, and treatment for shock (T-18). Everyone gets a tag (T-18).

next.question: Step 3, Mental status: can they follow a simple command?
detail: Ask if they know their name and what happened (T-17).
Give a simple command, such as "Squeeze my hand" (T-17).
Language barrier or hearing impairment: reach out with both hands and squeeze one of their hands. They will squeeze back if they can (T-14).

action.text: Tag IMMEDIATE ("I", red). Inability to respond means immediate treatment for shock is necessary: treat for shock. All survivors tagged Immediate get airway control, bleeding control, and treatment for shock (T-18). Everyone gets a tag (T-18).

next.question: Can they walk and talk without assistance?
detail: They have passed all tests (breathing under 30 per minute, color returns in under 2 seconds, follows simple commands).

action.text: Tag DELAYED ("D", yellow). Passes all tests but cannot walk, talk and move without assistance. Treatment can be delayed. Everyone gets a tag (T-18).
Tag MINOR ("M", green). Passes all tests and can walk and talk without assistance. They may be able to help rescuers with other survivors. Everyone gets a tag (T-18).

next.question: Reposition the airway. Are they breathing now?
detail: Use the head-tilt/chin-lift. If you suspect a head, neck or spinal injury, use the jaw-thrust instead (T-9).
If breathing is not restored on the first try, try again using the same method (T-10).

next.question: Step 1, Respirations: is the breathing rate more or less than 30 per minute?
detail: Abnormally rapid breathing (above 30 per minute) indicates shock (T-17).

action.text: Tag IMMEDIATE ("I", red). Treat for shock. All survivors tagged Immediate get airway control, bleeding control, and treatment for shock (T-18). Everyone gets a tag (T-18).

Blanch test: press the nailbed base or fleshy fingertip until it turns white, release, and time how long normal color takes to return (T-14, T-17).
The blanch test is not valid for children. Use mental status as the main indicator for children (T-14).

detail: Ask if they know their name and what happened (T-17).
Give a simple command, such as "Squeeze my hand" (T-17).
Language barrier or hearing impairment: reach out with both hands and squeeze one of their hands. They will squeeze back if they can (T-14).

action.text: Tag IMMEDIATE ("I", red). Inability to respond means immediate treatment for shock is necessary: treat for shock. All survivors tagged Immediate get airway control, bleeding control, and treatment for shock (T-18). Everyone gets a tag (T-18).

next.question: Can they walk and talk without assistance?
detail: They have passed all tests (breathing under 30 per minute, color returns in under 2 seconds, follows simple commands).

action.text: Tag DELAYED ("D", yellow). Passes all tests but cannot walk, talk and move without assistance. Treatment can be delayed. Everyone gets a tag (T-18).
Tag MINOR ("M", green). Passes all tests and can walk and talk without assistance. They may be able to help rescuers with other survivors. Everyone gets a tag (T-18).

options.label: No: still not breathing after 2 attempts

action.text: Status: Black. No breathing after two attempts to open the airway. Never abbreviate Black to the letter "D". Move on to the next survivor. (Illinois rule: CERT uses only the Black category here. See About & Sources.) Everyone gets a tag (T-18).

warnings.text: Rescuer safety is paramount during triage. Wear proper protective equipment.
Suspected hazmat or terrorist event: CERT volunteers do NOT respond. Leave the scene.
Triage, not treatment: too much focus on one injury is a triage pitfall.

review.text: The unit gives only "above/below 30 per minute" and "under/over 2 seconds". Exactly 30 breaths or exactly 2 seconds is not addressed. The radial pulse test is named as an alternative (T-14), but no pass/fail criterion is given.

The flow chart shows only "Follows simple commands: D Delayed" (T-21). The Minor branch (walks and talks without assistance) comes from the text on T-18. The unit says the blanch test is not valid for children but gives no pediatric thresholds.

The RPM text says to follow the steps "if they do not respond" to shake-and-shout (T-17), but also says to evaluate and tag everyone, including the walking wounded (T-18, T-19). Instructor to clarify how responsive survivors are assessed.
Decision flow transcribed from the flow chart image (T-21, repeated on T-10, T-13, T-15) and the text on T-17 and T-18. Verify against the printed unit.

steps.text: Stop, look, listen and think. Size up the situation. Think about your safety, capability and limitations, and decide if and how you will approach. Make a quick plan.

Conduct voice triage. Call out: "Emergency Response Team. If you can walk, come to the sound of my voice." Tell those who can walk to stay at a designated location. Ask them to help if you need it; they may also know where other survivors are.
Start where you stand and follow a systematic route. Start with the closest survivors and work outward.
Evaluate each survivor and tag or mark them Immediate, Delayed, Minor or Black. Evaluate and tag the walking wounded too.
Treat "Immediate" survivors right away: airway management, bleeding control, and treatment for shock.
Document triage results: for deploying resources, for survivor locations, and as a quick count of casualties by severity.

topics.title: Triage categories & tags

tables.title: Triage categories
rows: Life-threatening injuries (airway, uncontrolled bleeding, or shock) that need immediate attention to save their life. Rapid, life-saving treatment is urgent.
Injuries are not life-threatening and do not put their life at risk. They may need professional care, but treatment can be delayed.
Injuries are superficial, needing minor bandaging and observation. They can walk, talk and help themselves, and may be able to assist rescuers.

No breathing after two attempts to open the airway. Never abbreviate Black to the letter D. (The unit's wording and its other Black criterion are paraphrased under the Illinois rule; see About & Sources.)

items.text: Everyone gets a tag. This supports accountability when scenes are chaotic.
Move all injured survivors marked RED / I / Immediate first.
Label the medical treatment areas Immediate, Delayed and Minor, and/or use colored ground tarps for the categories. Areas for the Black category: see Local Protocols.

topics.localProtocol: Consult local protocols and policies on which label or mark local professional responders prefer (T-16).

items.text: Respirations, "30": position the airway; look, listen and feel; check the rate. Above 30 per minute: treat for shock, tag Immediate. Below 30: go to perfusion. Not breathing after 2 attempts to open the airway: Status: Black.

Perfusion, "2": look for obvious bleeding and control severe bleeding. Blanch test: color takes longer than 2 seconds to return, treat for shock and tag Immediate. Under 2 seconds: go to mental status.
Mental status, "Can / Can't Do": ask their name and what happened, and give a simple command ("Squeeze my hand"). Unable to respond: treat for shock, tag Immediate.
Blanch test: press the nailbed base or fleshy fingertip until it turns white, then release. Normal color should return within two seconds.
The blanch test is not valid for children. Use mental status as the main indicator.
The radial pulse test is an alternative to the blanch test and can be used in the dark or where it is cold.

topics.title: Open the airway (triage unit)
topics.summary: Head-tilt/chin-lift. If you suspect a head, neck or spinal injury, use the jaw-thrust.

steps.text: At arm's distance, touch the shoulder, shake, and shout "Can you hear me?"
If they do not or cannot respond, place the palm of one hand on the forehead.
Place two fingers of the other hand under the chin and tilt the jaw upward while tilting the head back slightly.
Put your ear over their mouth, looking toward their feet, with a hand on their abdomen.
Look for chest rise.
Listen for air exchange.
Feel for abdominal movement.

items.text: Jaw-thrust (suspected spinal injury): one hand on each side of the head, thumbs near the corners of the mouth pointed toward the chin, elbows for support. Slide your fingers under the angles of the jawbone without moving the head or neck. Thrust the jaw upward without moving the head or neck.
Not breathing after the first try: try again with the same method. Not restored on the second try: move on to the next injured person.
Keep the airway open: have a volunteer or a walking wounded survivor hold the head, or place soft objects (shoes, blankets, jackets) under the shoulders to raise them slightly.

review.text: The triage unit teaches head-tilt/chin-lift as the main method (T-9). The FEMA 2019 airway section teaches self-positioning, the recovery position and the jaw-thrust, with no head-tilt/chin-lift (3-6 to 3-8). Instructor to confirm which to teach.

topics.title: Control bleeding (triage unit)
topics.summary: Direct pressure stops 90% of most bleeding injuries, but can take 5 to 7 minutes. A pressure bandage lets you move on to the next survivor.

steps.text: Find the source(s) of bleeding.
Put on non-latex exam gloves.
Apply firm, steady pressure directly on the source. Press hard, even if it is painful.
Tie a pressure bandage over the dressing. Tie the end in a bow so it can be loosened (not cut) to check the wound, then retied.
If bleeding comes through the second layer, move to a tourniquet.
Tourniquet: place it at least two inches above the wound (closer to the torso). Not over a joint. Over clothing is OK.
Pull the strap through the buckle.
Twist the rod tightly until bleeding stops or slows significantly. This will be very painful.
Secure the rod.
If bleeding does not stop, place a second tourniquet above the first, closer to the torso.
Mark the time the tourniquet was placed, on their forehead if possible.

warnings.text: Do not use the same gloves or barrier on more than one person.
Leave the tourniquet uncovered (e.g., by blankets) if possible. Only a medical professional should loosen or remove a tourniquet.
Improvised tourniquets often fail. Use one only as a last resort, to at least slow the bleeding.

items.text: If a barrier becomes blood soaked, replace it. If possible, do not remove the first layer of gauze (it may interfere with clotting): add another layer on top and keep pressure. Do not let the layers get too bulky.
A bystander, or the survivor, can maintain pressure so you can move on to others.

review.text: Tourniquet placement differs. FEMA 2019: as high as possible on the injured limb, closest to the torso (3-4). Triage unit: at least two inches above the wound, not over a joint (T-12). The unit also adds: second tourniquet above the first, and mark the time (T-12). Both shown. Instructor to reconcile.

Soaked dressings: FEMA 3-4 says replace and do not layer; FEMA 3-11 says redress over it; the triage unit says replace, but try not to remove the first layer and add another layer on top (T-12). Instructor to reconcile.

FEMA 2019 says keep pressure until EMS takes over (3-4). The triage unit says to tie a pressure bandage (bow) or hand pressure to a bystander so you can move on (T-11, T-12). Context differs (mass casualty triage). Instructor to confirm.

topics.title: Treat for shock (triage unit)
topics.summary: If you are unsure whether a survivor is in shock, treat for shock.

steps.text: Lay the survivor on their back. Elevate the feet 6-10 inches above the level of the heart. Maintain an open airway.
Control obvious bleeding.
Maintain body temperature (e.g., cover the ground and the survivor with a blanket if needed).
Avoid rough or excessive handling unless you and the survivor are in immediate danger. No food or drink.

items.text: Main signs of shock: rapid and shallow breathing; capillary refill of more than 2 seconds; failure to follow simple commands such as "Squeeze my hand"; changes in skin color.
Shock is often hard to recognize. Someone in shock can be fully coherent and not complaining of pain.

review.text: The triage unit says to lay the survivor on their back and elevate the feet 6-10 inches, with no food or drink (T-14). FEMA 2019 shock guidance (3-5) covers avoiding rough handling and keeping body temperature, but does not include leg elevation. Instructor to confirm.

topics.title: Triage scene: hazmat, damage, treatment areas

items.text: Suspected hazmat or terrorist event: do not respond. Leave the scene to avoid harm and reduce the spread of contamination.
Light and moderate damage: search, triage, then rescue and transport survivors. Do NOT enter structures with heavy damage.
Transport teams, walking wounded or other volunteers take survivors to the matching treatment area. Move Immediate first.
CPR is not performed when there are many more survivors than rescuers.

topics.localProtocol: Handling and moving people in the Black category: see Local Protocols (Illinois rule).

items.text: Establish command and control of the incident area.
Conduct size-up and set-up.
Send survivors with relatively minor injuries to a holding area to await treatment.
Identify survivors who need life-saving intervention and treat them immediately.
Identify survivors in the Black category and those too severely injured to save.
Manage medical transportation for survivors who need more treatment.
Secure the area to protect responders, survivors, and evidence for law enforcement.
Remove debris and other safety or health threats.
No team plan, organization or goal
Indecisive leadership
Too much focus on one injury
Treatment (rather than triage) performed

topics.title: PPE and gloves during triage
topics.summary: Before treating anyone, have and use a helmet, goggles, gloves, an N95 mask, sturdy shoes or boots, and non-latex exam gloves. Carry multiple sets of gloves.

steps.text: If you run out of gloves: remove obvious soil from the gloves, preferably by washing with soap and water.
Mix 1 part unscented bleach (preferably less than a year old) to 10 parts water.
With the gloves still on, swish them in the solution for at least 6 seconds.

items.text: Practice removing non-latex gloves safely to avoid contaminating yourself.

review.text: Glove sterilization with 1:10 bleach for at least 6 seconds (T-6) does not appear in the FEMA 2019 manual. Instructor to confirm.

topics.title: Good Samaritan basics (as stated in the unit)

items.text: Do not practice outside the scope of your training.
Once you start medical assistance, do not stop unless absolutely necessary to help others or you become a survivor yourself.
Accept no compensation of any kind.
Act in good faith; no gross negligence.

topics.localProtocol: The unit does not cite a statute. Confirm the Illinois specifics with your program (FEMA Table 1.6, 1-26).

sections.title: Life-Threatening Conditions
sections.summary: First priority in medical ops: control severe bleeding, open the airway, and maintain body temperature.

steps.text: Is the spot safe? Stay and treat, or move to safety (and can you take anyone with you)?
Put on PPE when able.
If conscious, make sure the patient can see you.
Identify yourself by name and organization.
Ask permission to treat. Unconscious = implied consent. For a child, ask a parent or guardian if possible.
Respect cultural differences whenever possible.
Keep patients' medical information confidential.

items.text: Spurting or steady bleeding
Blood is pooling
Blood soaking through clothes
Blood soaking through bandages
Amputation

steps.text: Find the source(s) of bleeding.
Put a barrier between the blood and your hands if available (gloves best; cloth, plastic bag).
Apply firm, steady pressure directly on the source. Push hard, even if it is painful.
Keep pressure until EMS takes over or bleeding has stopped. If unsure, keep pressing and wait for EMS.

warnings.text: Do not use the same gloves or barrier on more than one person.
If the barrier becomes blood soaked, replace it; do not layer more on top.
Do not put bulky layers between your hands and the wound; it weakens pressure.

review.text: The manual contradicts itself on blood-soaked dressings: page 3-4 says replace the barrier and do not layer more on top; page 3-11 says redress over the soaked dressing and maintain pressure. The program's triage unit says replace it, but try not to remove the first layer and add another layer on top (T-12). All are shown. Instructor to reconcile.

topics.title: Tourniquet
topics.summary: Use when direct pressure can't stop the bleeding and EMS is delayed. You are more likely to save a life than cause loss of a limb.

steps.text: Place as high as possible on the injured limb, closest to the torso (over clothing is OK).
Pull the strap through the buckle.
Twist the rod tightly until bleeding stops or slows significantly (may be very painful).
Secure the rod.
If bleeding does not stop, place a second tourniquet.
Leave in place until EMS takes over care.

warnings.text: Improvised tourniquets often fail. Use one (webbed belt, luggage strap) only as a last resort to at least slow bleeding.

review.text: Tourniquet placement differs. FEMA 2019: as high as possible on the injured limb, closest to the torso (3-4). The program's triage unit says at least two inches above the wound, not over a joint, and to mark the time placed (T-12). Both shown. Instructor to reconcile.

topics.title: Recognize shock
topics.summary: Shock is hard to spot. A patient can be fully coherent and not complain of pain.

items.text: Rapid and shallow breathing
Capillary refill greater than 2 seconds
Failure to follow simple commands, such as "squeeze my hand"

warnings.text: Avoid rough or excessive handling. Maintain body temperature.

review.text: The program's triage unit adds: lay on back, elevate feet 6-10 inches, no food or drink (T-14), and lists "changes in skin color" as a shock sign (T-13). These are not in FEMA 2019 (3-5). Instructor to confirm.

steps.text: Remove wet clothing.
Put something between the person and the ground (cardboard, jacket, blanket).
Wrap in dry layers (coat, blanket, Mylar emergency blanket).
Shield from wind with your body or surrounding objects.

topics.title: Open the airway

action.text: Let them position themselves and self-manage the airway; assist if needed. Tripod position: sitting, legs shoulder-width, elbows/hands on knees, lean forward slightly; or standing, hands on knees, arms straight, lean forward with flat back.

notes: This course does not teach CPR (3-1). If an obstruction is suspected in an unconscious patient, use the jaw-thrust (3-7).

review.text: Transcribed from a figure (image) in the manual. Verify against printed page 3-7.

The program's triage unit uses head-tilt/chin-lift (T-9) and, during triage, assigns Status: Black after two failed airway attempts without CPR (T-16, T-17). The FEMA chart here says to perform CPR if you know it (3-7). Context differs (one patient vs. mass casualty). Instructor to confirm.

steps.text: Body laid on its side.
Bottom arm reached outward.
Top arm: hand rests on bicep of bottom arm.
Head rests on hand.
Legs bent slightly.
Chin raised forward.
Mouth pointed downward.

warnings.text: Support the head and neck when rolling; do not move them more than necessary.

topics.title: Jaw-thrust maneuver (adult)
topics.summary: Unconscious patient with suspected airway obstruction.

steps.text: Kneel above the patient's head.
One hand on each side of the head, thumbs near corners of the mouth pointing toward the chin, elbows for support.
Slide fingers under the angles of the jawbone without moving the head or neck.
Thrust the jaw upward without moving the head or neck to open the airway.

items.text: Share names; ask: How can I help? What do you need? What happened?
Tell them what you know (no speculating), what's being done, what happens next.
Keep them warm; offer a hand; keep eye contact; be patient.
If you must move on to help someone else, tell them.

review.text: Table 3.1 gives Stage II blood loss as 15%-40%; the text on the same page says 15%-30%. Both are shown.

sections.title: Basic First Aid
sections.summary: Care for common non-life-threatening injuries after life threats are handled.

topics.title: Heat burns
topics.summary: Size up first: What caused it? Is the danger still present? When did burning stop? Goals: prevent hypothermia, manage pain, reduce infection.

steps.text: Remove from the source. Put out flames; remove smoldering clothing unless stuck to skin.
Assess size and severity first (rapid cooling can cause shock), then cool hot skin or clothing: immerse in cool water no more than 1 minute, or use clean cool wet compresses.
Cover loosely with dry, sterile dressings.
Severe hand/foot burns: wrap fingers and toes loosely and individually.
Loosen clothing near the burn; remove jewelry if needed and note what, when, and to whom you gave it.

warnings.text: Do NOT use ice.
Do NOT apply antiseptics, ointments, or other remedies.
Do NOT remove shreds of tissue, break blisters, or remove adhered clothing (cut around it).

topics.title: Chemical burns
topics.summary: Suspect if skin is burning and there is no sign of fire. Best to defer to trained medical professionals.

steps.text: Protect yourself: goggles, mask, gloves.
Remove affected clothing and jewelry.
If dry, gently brush away, away from eyes, patient, and yourself.
Flush with lots of cool running water for at least 10 minutes.
Apply a cool, wet compress for pain.
Cover very loosely with dry, sterile or clean cloth.

tables.title: Table 3.2: Burn Classification
rows: Reddened, dry skin; pain; possible swelling
Reddened, blistered skin; wet appearance; pain; possible swelling
Complete destruction of epidermis and dermis; possible subcutaneous damage
Whitened, leathery, or charred (brown or black); painful or relatively painless

steps.text: Control bleeding first.
Apply a dressing (sterile when possible) directly to the wound.
Bandage holds the dressing; if still bleeding, bandage firmly enough to help control bleeding without cutting off circulation.
If dressing is soaked (active bleeding), redress over it and maintain pressure.
No active bleeding: keep pressure and keep bandaged until medical professional treatment.

items.text: Infection signs: swelling, discoloration, discharge, red striations from the wound

warnings.text: Put nothing on wounds other than purified water; other solutions (e.g., hydrogen peroxide) are for trained medical personnel to decide.

review.text: The manual contradicts itself on blood-soaked dressings: page 3-4 says replace the barrier and do not layer more on top; page 3-11 says redress over the soaked dressing and maintain pressure. The program's triage unit says replace it, but try not to remove the first layer and add another layer on top (T-12). All are shown. Instructor to reconcile.

topics.title: Amputations

steps.text: Never amputate a body part.
Wrap tissue in clean material, in a plastic bag if available, and label it (date, time, patient name).
Keep tissue cool but NOT in direct contact with ice.
Keep the severed part with the patient.

notes: The label is written on the bag. The app must not record the patient's name.

topics.title: Impaled objects
topics.summary: Usually outside CERT scope; get EMS. If EMS is far or unavailable:

steps.text: Immobilize the affected body part.
Do not move or remove the object unless it obstructs the airway.
Control bleeding at the entrance wound without pressing on the object.
Clean and dress the wound, stabilizing the object.
Wrap bulky dressings around the object to keep it from moving.

topics.title: Fractures, dislocations, sprains
topics.summary: If unsure which it is, treat as a fracture. Immobilize the injury and the joints above and below.

steps.text: Closed fracture, dislocation, sprain or strain: treat as closed fracture, so splint.
Open fracture (higher priority, check more often): cover with sterile dressing and apply pressure; splint without disturbing the wound; place a moist 4x4 dressing over the bone end.
Remove restrictive clothing, shoes, jewelry so they don't act as tourniquets.

items.text: Sprain signs: tenderness, swelling and/or bruising, restricted or lost use

warnings.text: Open fracture: do NOT draw bone ends back into tissue; do NOT irrigate.
Do not try to relocate a dislocation; immobilize it.

items.text: Cardboard (most common): turn up edges to form a mold for the limb.
Towel: roll and wrap around limb, tie in place.
Pillow: wrap and tie around limb.
Anatomical: tie injured leg to uninjured leg at intervals with blanket padding between.
Rigid options: board, metal strip, folded magazine/newspaper.
Fill gaps between splint and body with soft material.

steps.text: Remove wet clothing.
Insulate from the ground.
Wrap in dry layers.
Shield from wind.
Place an unconscious patient in the recovery position.

items.text: Signs: body temperature 95°F (35°C) or lower; redness or blueness of skin; numbness with shivering. Later: slurred speech, unpredictable behavior, listlessness.

warnings.text: Do not use massage to warm body parts.

corrections.text: The manual prints "95º F (37º C)". 95°F is 35°C, so the Celsius value is shown corrected here.

steps.text: Warm slowly: immerse in warm (NOT hot) water, about 107.6°F.
Wrap affected parts in dry, sterile dressing.

items.text: Signs: skin discoloration (red, white, purple, black); burning or tingling; partial or complete numbness. Most common in nose, ears, hands, feet.

warnings.text: Do NOT let the part re-freeze.
Do NOT massage or rub.

steps.text: Move out of the heat to a cool environment.
Cool slowly with cool, wet towels or sheets; cool bath if possible.
Give water SLOWLY: about half a glass every 15 minutes.
If vomiting, cramping, or losing consciousness: NO food or drink; alert a medical professional; watch closely.

tables.title: Heat illness signs
rows: Cool, moist, pale or flushed skin; heavy sweating; headache; nausea/vomiting; dizziness; exhaustion; near-normal temperature
Hot, red skin; lack of perspiration; changes in consciousness; rapid weak pulse; rapid shallow breathing; temp can reach 105°F

warnings.text: Untreated heat exhaustion becomes heat stroke.

steps.text: Scrape out the stinger with a credit card edge. Not tweezers.
Wash with soap and water.
Wrapped ice on 10 minutes, off 10 minutes; repeat.

warnings.text: Anaphylaxis (airway compromised): calm the person; find and help administer their own Epi-pen. Give NO other medicine.

sections.title: Disaster Medical Operations
sections.summary: Assessment, treatment areas, mass casualty roles, and public health.

topics.title: Your role at a mass casualty incident

steps.text: Conduct a scene size-up.
Call 9-1-1 with your size-up information.
Put on PPE and CERT-affiliated gear (hat, vest, shirt).
Find the nearest first responder; identify yourself as CERT and give your local agency affiliation.
If no responder is available, decide whether you can provide life-saving interventions (bleeding, airway).
When responders arrive, give them your size-up details and ask how to help.
If asked to leave, leave; then report the incident and your role to your CERT TL / local agency.

topics.title: Medical operations functions

tables.title: Functions of disaster medical operations
rows: Initial assessment and sorting of survivors by injury severity
Moving survivors from scene to treatment area or medical facility
Hub for getting and distributing supplies

notes: The manual names Triage/Assessment as a function but gives no triage protocol or tag categories. Use the method your local program specifies (see Local Protocols).
The manual lists one more area. It is covered under Local Protocols (Illinois rule).

items.text: Located a safe distance from, but not too far from, damage sites.
Accessible by transport vehicles; expandable.
Physically separate the survivor treatment areas. Other areas: see Local Protocols.
Light damage: assess as found; further treatment in a safe location inside designated areas.
Moderate damage: assess as found; send to a treatment area a safe distance away.
Heavy damage: never enter.

topics.title: Head-to-toe assessment
topics.summary: Do on all survivors, even those who seem fine. Treat life threats FIRST. Do the full assessment before treating other injuries. Do it the same way every time.

steps.text: Wear PPE. If conscious, ask permission (patient may refuse) and talk to reduce anxiety.
Ask about injuries, pain, bleeding, symptoms. Be verbal and hands-on; remove clothing to look if needed.
Check each area for DCAP-BTLS, in order: 1 Head, 2 Neck, 3 Shoulders, 4 Chest, 5 Arms, 6 Abdomen, 7 Pelvis, 8 Legs.
Check Pulse, Movement, Sensation (PMS) in all extremities.
Look for medical ID emblems (bracelet or necklace).
Check your own hands for the patient's blood as you go.
Note how they were hurt; it hints at likely injuries.

warnings.text: Suspect spinal injury in ALL unconscious survivors.

steps.text: Do no harm: minimize head and spine movement while treating life threats.
Improvise a backboard (door, desktop, building materials).
Tuck towels, drapes, or clothing snugly on both sides of the head to immobilize.
Use log rolling to move onto a board: rescuer at the head gives commands; roll as a single unit.
Move only for safety, or when help is delayed and a treatment area is set up.

items.text: Signs: change in consciousness; can't move body part(s); severe head/neck/back pain or pressure; tingling or numbness in extremities; difficulty breathing or seeing; heavy bleeding, bruising, or deformity of head/spine; blood or fluid in ears/nose; bruising behind the ear; "raccoon" eyes; uneven pupils; seizures; nausea or vomiting.
Also treat as spinal if found under collapsed building material or heavy debris.

warnings.text: If rescuer or patient is in immediate danger, safety outweighs possible spinal injury; move quickly.

items.text: Wash hands 15-20 seconds, all surfaces; or alcohol sanitizer (at least 60% alcohol, about 1/2 teaspoon, rub until dry).
Wear non-latex exam gloves at all times; change or disinfect between patients. Field option: rubber gloves sterilized in 1 part bleach to 10 parts water.
Keep dressings sterile until use; use the entire package once opened if possible.
Wash areas contacted by body fluids with soap and water or diluted bleach.
Bag, tie, and mark medical waste; keep separate; dispose as hazardous waste.
Bury human waste away from operations; mark the site.
Boil at a rolling boil for 1 minute, or use purification tablets, or non-perfumed liquid bleach.
Bleach must be plain 5.25-6.0% sodium hypochlorite; not perfumed.
After adding bleach, mix and let stand 30 minutes.
If it doesn't smell of bleach, add 6 more drops and let stand 15 minutes.

sections.title: Disaster Psychology
sections.summary: Psychological first aid: stabilize people, listen, protect, connect, and look after your team.

steps.text: Address medical needs first.
Observe responsiveness; decide if they're a danger to self or others.
Get uninjured people involved in constructive jobs (e.g., organizing supplies). This works especially well for disruptive survivors.
Support by listening, empathizing, and connecting them to family, friends, or clergy.
LISTEN: pay attention to what they say, how they act, what they need now. Okay if they don't want to talk; check back regularly.

PROTECT: give information and resources; answer simply and honestly; let them know they're not alone; don't force talk; explain what's being done for safety; reduce re-traumatizing sights, smells, sounds; help identify basic needs.
CONNECT: help reconnect with friends and loved ones; check in regularly; help find support resources.

warnings.text: Survivors who seem suicidal, psychotic, or unable to care for themselves: refer to EMS and/or mental health professionals as soon as possible.

items.text: Always ask permission to enter their space, help, or interact.
It's okay to apologize; be comfortable with silence.

tables.title: Words (columns are independent lists)
rows: "Is it all right if I help you with...?"
"I can't imagine what this is like for you."
"It could be worse" / "At least you still have..." / "Everything will be okay."

items.text: Brief personnel beforehand on what to expect.
Emphasize the team; share the workload.
Enforce rest, breaks away from the incident area, and rotation (high- to low-stress jobs).
Encourage eating and fluids: water or electrolyte drinks; avoid caffeine and refined sugar.
Watch teammates for stress changes.
Don't send volunteers home straight from high-stress work; assign low-stress tasks first.
Hold a brief discussion after each shift.
5 Fs: Freeze, Flight, Fight, Fright, Faint.
Physical: loss of appetite; headaches or chest pain; diarrhea, stomach pain, nausea; hyperactivity; more alcohol or drug use; nightmares; can't sleep; fatigue.
Vicarious trauma: over-identifying with survivors. Don't take on their feelings as your own.
Pre-disaster, Impact, Heroic, Honeymoon, Disillusionment, Reconstruction.

sections.title: Fire Safety & Suppression
sections.summary: Small fires only. If you can't put it out in 5 seconds, leave.

items.text: If you cannot put out a fire in five seconds, it is too big. Leave immediately.

topics.title: Fire size-up: 5 questions

items.text: Do my buddy and I have the right equipment?
Are there other hazards?
Is the building structurally damaged?
Can my buddy and I escape?
Can my buddy and I fight the fire safely?
(Size-up Step 3 adds) Does the path of the fire jeopardize other areas?

notes: The full 9-step fire size-up worksheet (Table 6.1) mirrors the general worksheet (2-9/2-10) with the added 'Path of Fire' item.

topics.title: Should I use an extinguisher?
topics.summary: Image 6.3. Any NO means leave immediately.

sequence.text: Can I escape quickly and safely if I don't succeed? (two ways out)
Do I have the right type of extinguisher?
Is the extinguisher large enough for the fire?
Is the area free of other dangers (hazardous materials, falling debris)?
Am I experienced or trained in using an extinguisher?
START TO EXTINGUISH. Is the fire out within 5 seconds?

onNo.text: LEAVE IMMEDIATELY: activate fire alarm if safe; shut doors behind you; contact fire department.

onAllYes.text: Stay and overhaul if the area is safe ("cool, soak, and separate"). Contact the fire department anyway.

warnings.text: Even if every answer is YES, leave if you feel unable to extinguish the fire.

review.text: Transcribed from a figure (image) in the manual. Verify against printed page 6-9.

topics.title: P.A.S.S.

steps.text: PULL the pin, then TEST the extinguisher before approaching the fire.
AIM at the base of the fire (the fuel, not the flames).
SQUEEZE the handle.
SWEEP side to side at the base.

notes: Lay fully depleted extinguishers on their side so no one tries to use them before recharge (6-11).

topics.title: Two-person suppression procedure
topics.summary: Team Member 1 (TM1) operates the extinguisher. Team Member 2 (TM2) watches for hazards and protects TM1.

steps.text: Ready position: pin pulled, extinguisher upright and aimed, about 20-25 feet from a small fire.
TM1: "Ready." TM2 repeats "Ready."
TM1: "Going in." TM2 repeats and stays within reach.
Walk in together. TM1 watches the fire; TM2 keeps a hand on TM1's shoulder.
TM1: "Backing out." TM2 repeats.
TM2 guides TM1 out by hand; TM1 keeps facing the fire. Never turn your back on it.

notes: Exercise 6.1 (6-22) adds: approach from the windward side (wind at your back) and begin discharging at about 10 feet, continuing to optimal range. This comes from a training exercise.

items.text: Wear safety equipment at all times; if not equipped, leave.
Work with a buddy; have a backup team whenever possible.
Always have two ways out.
Look at the door: air sucked under or smoke at the top means do not touch or open it.
Feel closed doors with the back of your hand, bottom to top and the frame, before touching the handle. Hot door = fire behind; do not enter.
Confine fire by closing doors.
Stay low.
Keep a safe distance (outer range of the extinguisher).
Never turn your back on a fire when backing out.
Overhaul so it stays out.

warnings.text: DO NOT get too close; if you feel the heat, you're too close.
DO NOT fight a fire alone.
DO NOT try to suppress large fires (e.g., larger than combined extinguisher ratings).
DO NOT enter smoke-filled areas.
Never operate interior wet standpipes.

items.text: Label ratings: Class A 1A-40A; Class B 1B-640B (higher = more agent). C, D, K have no number; "C" means safe on electrical fires.

tables.title: Fire classes
rows: Ordinary combustibles: paper, cloth, wood, rubber, many plastics
Flammable/combustible liquids: oils, gasoline, lighter fluid, kerosene (only vapor burns)
Energized electrical equipment (becomes Class A when power is off)

tables.title: Fire type, agent, method (Table 6.2)
rows: Removes heat; removes air and heat; breaks chain reaction

warnings.text: Water extinguishers can scatter lightweight burning material and spread fire.
Only use a Class B-rated extinguisher on flammable liquids.

sections.title: Utility Controls
sections.summary: Shut off utilities only when necessary and safe.

topics.title: Natural gas shutoff

steps.text: Outside meter: if you smell gas or dials show flow with appliances off, turn off at the meter.
Use a non-sparking wrench; turn the valve on the pipe coming out of the ground one-quarter turn clockwise.
Use a flashlight, never a candle, for light.
If there's a fire you can't extinguish: call 9-1-1; shut off gas only if safe.

warnings.text: Meter INSIDE the home: shut off only when instructed by local authorities. If you smell gas, evacuate and call 9-1-1. Do not shut off from inside if gas may be in the air.
Never enter the basement of a burning structure to turn off a utility.
Only a licensed/trained technician may turn gas back on.
If unsure how to shut off safely, don't. Contact the gas company.

notes: Some meters have automatic (earthquake) shutoff valves; only a qualified professional restores them (6-16).
Multi-unit dwellings may have a building main plus per-unit shutoffs (1-8).
topics.localProtocol: Always follow your local fire department's guidelines (6-17).

steps.text: Switch off smaller breakers (or unscrew individual fuses) first.
Then pull the main switch or breaker.
To restore: main first, then the smaller breakers/fuses one at a time.
Notify a licensed electrician and/or utility company.

warnings.text: Do not enter a flooded basement or wade into standing water to shut off power.

items.text: Natural gas is an asphyxiant and flammable; lighter than air.
CO is deadly, colorless, odorless; lighter than air; from incomplete burning (generators, furnaces, charcoal indoors).
Read labels; store using L.I.E.S. (Limit, Isolate, Eliminate, Separate).

topics.title: Water shutoff
topics.summary: The manual says to locate, label, and know how to shut off water (1-12, 1-21) but gives NO water shutoff procedure.
topics.localProtocol: Get the procedure from your local program or utility if you want to include it.

sections.title: Hazardous Materials & CBRNE
sections.summary: Placards are a STOP SIGN. Stay away, stay upwind, call professionals.

steps.text: Treat placards (NFPA 704, DOT, UN, NA) as a STOP SIGN.
Treat any unknown situation as a hazmat incident; no placard doesn't mean no hazmat.
Only action: evacuate people who are downwind to an uphill or upwind location.
Do not enter the building to evacuate people inside.
Stay away from unidentified substances; alert authorities; call for professional help.

warnings.text: Placards aren't required under 1,000 lbs for many materials, and may be wrong or outdated. Use extreme caution at any vehicle accident.

tables.title: NFPA 704 quadrants (0-4, higher = more risk)
rows: Special precautions: W (water-reactive), OX (oxidizer), ACID, ALK, COR, radioactive symbol

items.text: Elements: pictogram symbols, signal word ("Danger" severe / "Warning" less severe), hazard statements.

steps.text: Leave the area: go inside, outside, or upwind/uphill/upstream, at least 1,000-1,500 feet.
Seconds count. Remove everything including jewelry; cut off clothing that would come off over the head; seal clothes in a plastic bag.
Wash hands first, then flush whole body (eyes, underarms, groin) with lots of COOL water. Soap and water if available, no scrubbing.
Wash hair with soap/shampoo or rinse; no conditioner.
Blot dry (don't rub); put on clean clothes.

warnings.text: If hosing someone else, avoid contact with them and the runoff; contain or drain decon water away from shelter.

steps.text: Do not touch it.
Move away.
Report to authorities immediately.

items.text: Unusual vapor clouds or mists for the area or time of day.
Out-of-place, unattended packages, boxes, or vehicles.

steps.text: Shut off ventilation; latch doors and windows.
Go to your shelter room (pre-cut plastic, duct tape, radio, supplies).
Cover doors, windows, vents, outlets with plastic extending several inches past edges; tape all around.
Seal gaps under doors and pipe entries (towels plus tape).
Monitor Emergency Alert System; usually no more than a few hours.
When clear, open windows and vents, run fans.

items.text: Air: 10 sq ft of floor per person is enough for up to 5 hours at rest.

steps.text: Get inside, stay inside, stay tuned (time, distance, shielding).
Go deep inside: farthest interior room or basement; avoid top floor or floors next to flat roofs.
If outside: don't look at the flash; take cover, lie flat, cover head; get inside ASAP.

tables.title: Zones
rows: Upwind/upstream; decon and isolation, or area just outside scene
Beyond warm zone; survivors held until released by responders

sections.title: Light Search & Rescue
sections.summary: Size-up, then search, then rescue. Rescue the greatest number in the shortest time without risking rescuers.

items.text: Decide on: risks to rescuer and survivor; greatest good for greatest number; resources and labor available.
Goals in order: get walking wounded and ambulatory out first; then lightly trapped; keep rescuers and survivors safe.
Priority basis: CERT safety; life safety; protect environment; protect property.
Remove or mitigate known hazards before searching.
Facts: time of day/week (night means residences; day means workplaces); construction type and terrain; occupancy; weather; hazards (e.g., shut off a suspected gas leak first).
Damage: take a lap around the building. Beyond CERT capability? Communicated?
Probabilities: Is it stable? More disaster activity likely? What else could go wrong? Need a spotter for collapse movement?
Your situation: personnel, equipment, tools available? Can CERT do this safely? If no, don't.
Plan: written plan recommended for S&R; note changes.
Evaluate progress: the most critical step for safety.
A = front of building; B, C, D go clockwise from A.
Interior quadrants named by nearest sides, e.g., A/B quadrant.

tables.title: Table 7.2 (earthquake)
rows: Broken glass; content movement; exterior trim and fascia

steps.text: Signs of life in a STRUCTURAL void: report to TL immediately and mark for professionals. Do NOT attempt the rescue.
Ask bystanders: How many live/work here? Where would they be now? Layout? What have you seen or heard? Has anyone come out? Normal exits?

items.text: Structural voids: pancake, lean-to, V.
Individual voids: bathtubs, under desks; children may hide in cabinets.

warnings.text: Collapsed floors or walls: leave the premises immediately.
Bystanders may exaggerate or misremember.

steps.text: On ENTRY: mark next to the door (not on the door, not where it swings). Draw a single slash.
Write agency/group ID at the 9 o'clock (left) position.
Write date and time IN at the 12 o'clock (top) position.
On EXIT: draw the second slash to form an X. Write time OUT in the top quadrant.
Right quadrant: areas searched and hazard information.
Bottom quadrant: survivor counts, using the manual's L and D letters (L = living). For the D count, follow Local Protocols (Illinois rule). Note where survivors were taken.
Front-of-building mark shows total survivors; interior marks show totals per area.

review.text: The manual describes search markings in text only (no diagram). The app graphic is drawn from that text, and the manual does not say which slash comes first.

steps.text: Stay within arm's reach of a buddy.
Call out on entering each space: "If anyone can hear my voice, come here." Ask those who come for info; then direct them: "Stay here" or "Wait outside."
Give simple directions in short sentences while looking directly at the person.
Use a systematic pattern: bottom-up/top-down or right wall/left wall.
Check all six sides of each space, including ceiling and floor.
Stop frequently to listen for tapping, movement, voices.
Triangulate if location is obscured (3 rescuers, flashlights from different angles). Not an initial method.
Record survivors removed, still trapped, and in the Black category (per triage); report to emergency services.

topics.title: Exterior (grid) search

steps.text: Assemble at staging and sign in; get a briefing from those in charge.
Line up on one side of the grid; spacing set by visibility and debris.
Keep line of sight and voice contact with searchers on both sides; overlap coverage.
Move across in as straight a line as possible; search your row thoroughly.
Record each area searched.

notes: Other patterns: line, quadrant/zone, spiral (7-16). Protect evidence if it may be a crime scene (7-16).
topics.localProtocol: Exterior searches follow procedures set by those in charge of the search (7-16).

items.text: Work in pairs.
Light damage: assess and treat. Moderate damage: assess only; remove survivors quickly.
Never enter an unstable structure.
Lift by bending knees, back straight, push with legs; carry close; no more than reasonable.
Remove debris to reduce risk and free survivors; use a human chain that doesn't block the rescue.

topics.title: Leveraging & cribbing
topics.summary: "Lift an inch, crib an inch." Lever and fulcrum must be perpendicular (90°) to the edge being lifted.

steps.text: Size up: gather facts, identify hazards, set priorities.
One person in charge; plan where to lift and crib and how to remove the survivor.
Gather lever, fulcrum, cribbing blocks, spacers/wedges (improvise if needed).
Crib to stabilize the object before lifting.
Stage cribbing within reach.
Set lever and fulcrum at the chosen spot.
Assign a person to monitor and remove the survivor.
Lift using the lever and fulcrum.
Add cribbing one layer at a time as it rises.
When adequately supported, remove lever and fulcrum; remove the survivor.
Unless you must evacuate, re-lift and remove cribbing in reverse order.
Lower the object progressively to a stable position.
Collect supplies for the next operation.

tables.title: Team positions (Image 7.2)
rows: In front of the collapse; sees whole operation, out of the way
Front edge; places fulcrum and lever
Either side; place cribbing as it rises
Next to the crib person nearest the survivor's head

tables.title: Box cribbing
rows: Two pieces parallel on either side
Add layers, each perpendicular to the last

warnings.text: Never lever and crib at opposite ends at the same time. Do one end, then the other.
Too sharp a lever angle is inefficient and can cause back injury.

topics.title: Survivor removal: carries & drags
topics.summary: Choose by environment stability, number and strength of rescuers, and survivor condition. Let ambulatory survivors self-extricate (they may need help). Suspected head/spine injury: backboard, not lifts or drags, if safety and time permit.

tables.title: Removal methods
rows: Small survivor: reach around back and under knees; lift with legs
Back to survivor; their arms over your shoulders, grab hands at your chest; bend forward until their feet clear. Short distances.
R1 at head: from behind, reach under arms, grasp survivor's opposite wrists (crossed). R2 between knees, grasp outside of legs at knees. Rise together.
Sturdy non-swivel chair; survivor's arms crossed in lap. R1 grasps back upright, R2 front legs; tilt back, lift together.
Log roll onto blanket; roll edges as handles; lead calls "Ready to lift on the count of three"; carry feet first, level; lower on command.
For suspected spinal injury; rescuer at head commands; roll as one unit onto blanket/board.
Grasp feet or shoulders and drag clear; or wrap in blanket, grasp edge behind head, drag.

warnings.text: Over stairs or uneven ground, carriers must face each other.
Put stronger rescuers at the upper body.

sections.title: Terrorism & Active Shooter
sections.summary: CERT volunteers do NOT activate for terrorist incidents. Protect yourself; help only if you find yourself there.

items.text: CERT volunteers are NOT equipped or trained to respond to terrorist incidents and should in no way activate or respond.
If you are caught in one: follow law enforcement and first responders; your safety first; save lives if you can.

steps.text: RUN: if there's an escape path, go, whether or not others follow. Leave belongings; help others if possible; keep others from entering; hands visible; follow police; call 9-1-1 when safe.

HIDE: out of view, protected, not trapping you. Lock and barricade the door; silence phone; turn off noise; hide behind large items; stay quiet. If you can't speak, dial 9-1-1 and leave the line open.
FIGHT: last resort when life is in imminent danger. Act decisively and aggressively, throw items, improvise weapons, yell, commit.

items.text: Stay calm; follow instructions; put down items; raise hands, fingers spread; keep hands visible.
No quick movements toward officers; no pointing or yelling; don't stop to ask for help. Exit the way officers came in.
Tell 9-1-1/police: shooter location, number, description, weapons, number of potential victims.
Stay at the assembly point until released.
Focus on Unit 3 life-savers: stop bleeding, maintain body temperature, open airway, provide comfort.
Blast injuries: overpressure (blast lung is the leading cause of illness and death in initial survivors), fragments, impact, thermal, toxic or crush injuries.
Watch for secondary attacks aimed at caregivers; move away from danger and take others if you can.
Secondary hazards: fire, toxic smoke, power loss, ruptured gas and water lines, debris, traffic.

Surveillance; Elicitation; Tests of security; Funding; Acquiring supplies; Impersonation / people who don't belong; Rehearsal and dry runs; Deployment. Report to local law enforcement (FBI tips: tips.fbi.gov).

sections.title: Personal Preparedness
sections.summary: Before a disaster: your plan, your kit, your CERT gear.

items.text: Nylon or canvas bag with shoulder strap
Water (two canteens or bottles per search and rescue team)
Dehydrated foods
Water purification tablets
Non-latex exam gloves (10 pair minimum)
Flashlight or miner's lamp, plus secondary flashlight
Batteries and extra bulbs
Cyalume stick (12-hour omni glow)
Voltage tick meter
Pealess whistle
Utility knife
Notepads; markers (thin and thick point)
Pens
Duct tape; two-inch masking tape
Scissors (EMT shears)
Non-sparking crescent wrench
First aid pouch: 4x4 gauze (6), abdominal pads (4), triangular bandages (4), Band-Aids, roller bandage
Any personal medications you may need
Two meeting places: near home, and outside the neighborhood.
Out-of-state check-in contact.
Plan for extended stay, shelter in place, or evacuation; escape routes and alternates.
Show responsible family members how and when to shut off water, gas, electricity.
Smoke alarm on each level; CO alarm near bedrooms; test monthly.
Meet with neighbors; know their skills; plan childcare.
At least 1 gallon per person per day (3 qt drinking, 1 qt prep/sanitation); at least a 3-day supply.
Use #1 plastic bottles; replace every 6 months.
At least a 3-day supply of nonperishable food.

topics.title: Home disaster kit checklist
topics.summary: Full checklist on 1-34 to 1-37 (food, kitchen, first aid, meds, tools, sanitation, clothing, documents, infants, pets on 1-16).
notes: Good candidate for an offline, on-device-only checklist. Do not upload.

items.text: Shelter in place: seal an internal room for a few hours.
Extended stay: several days (up to two weeks for pandemic).
Mass care shelter: bring your 3-day kit.
A safe room (high wind) is not the same as a shelter-in-place room.

topics.title: Protection for volunteers

items.text: Good Samaritan laws generally protect volunteers who give care prudently and reasonably.
Volunteer Protection Act of 1997 protects volunteers acting within their training; state statutes may add protection.
When you put on the green CERT vest, you represent your sponsoring agency.

app.illinoisRule: Illinois rule: a non-medical professional may pronounce a person's death only in cases of decapitation. CERT still uses the Black triage category, so this app uses only "Black" (for example "Status: Black") for that outcome. Where a source uses other wording, the app paraphrases it.

corrections.title: Hypothermia threshold
corrections.text: Manual page 3-16 prints "95º F (37º C)". 95°F equals 35°C (37°C is normal body temperature). The app shows 95°F (35°C).

reviewFlags.title: Required PPE
reviewFlags.text: PPE lists differ across the manual (1-25, 1-31, and 6-12, which says "dust mask"). This list combines 1-25 and 1-31.

reviewFlags.title: Team tasks by damage level
reviewFlags.text: Transcribed from a figure (image) in the manual. Verify against printed page 2-11.

reviewFlags.title: Team size & span of control
reviewFlags.text: Page 2-5 says operations teams are 1-5 people, and also that search & rescue teams need at least 4. Both are shown.

reviewFlags.title: Response team report categories
reviewFlags.text: Transcribed from a figure (image) in the manual. Verify against printed page 2-17.

reviewFlags.title: START triage decision
reviewFlags.text: The unit gives only "above/below 30 per minute" and "under/over 2 seconds". Exactly 30 breaths or exactly 2 seconds is not addressed. The radial pulse test is named as an alternative (T-14), but no pass/fail criterion is given.

reviewFlags.title: START triage decision
reviewFlags.text: The flow chart shows only "Follows simple commands: D Delayed" (T-21). The Minor branch (walks and talks without assistance) comes from the text on T-18. The unit says the blanch test is not valid for children but gives no pediatric thresholds.

reviewFlags.title: START triage decision
reviewFlags.text: The RPM text says to follow the steps "if they do not respond" to shake-and-shout (T-17), but also says to evaluate and tag everyone, including the walking wounded (T-18, T-19). Instructor to clarify how responsive survivors are assessed.

reviewFlags.title: START triage decision
reviewFlags.text: Decision flow transcribed from the flow chart image (T-21, repeated on T-10, T-13, T-15) and the text on T-17 and T-18. Verify against the printed unit.

reviewFlags.title: Open the airway (triage unit)
reviewFlags.text: The triage unit teaches head-tilt/chin-lift as the main method (T-9). The FEMA 2019 airway section teaches self-positioning, the recovery position and the jaw-thrust, with no head-tilt/chin-lift (3-6 to 3-8). Instructor to confirm which to teach.

reviewFlags.title: Control bleeding (triage unit)
reviewFlags.text: Tourniquet placement differs. FEMA 2019: as high as possible on the injured limb, closest to the torso (3-4). Triage unit: at least two inches above the wound, not over a joint (T-12). The unit also adds: second tourniquet above the first, and mark the time (T-12). Both shown. Instructor to reconcile.

reviewFlags.title: Control bleeding (triage unit)
reviewFlags.text: Soaked dressings: FEMA 3-4 says replace and do not layer; FEMA 3-11 says redress over it; the triage unit says replace, but try not to remove the first layer and add another layer on top (T-12). Instructor to reconcile.

reviewFlags.title: Control bleeding (triage unit)
reviewFlags.text: FEMA 2019 says keep pressure until EMS takes over (3-4). The triage unit says to tie a pressure bandage (bow) or hand pressure to a bystander so you can move on (T-11, T-12). Context differs (mass casualty triage). Instructor to confirm.

reviewFlags.title: Treat for shock (triage unit)
reviewFlags.text: The triage unit says to lay the survivor on their back and elevate the feet 6-10 inches, with no food or drink (T-14). FEMA 2019 shock guidance (3-5) covers avoiding rough handling and keeping body temperature, but does not include leg elevation. Instructor to confirm.

reviewFlags.title: PPE and gloves during triage
reviewFlags.text: Glove sterilization with 1:10 bleach for at least 6 seconds (T-6) does not appear in the FEMA 2019 manual. Instructor to confirm.

reviewFlags.title: Direct pressure
reviewFlags.text: The manual contradicts itself on blood-soaked dressings: page 3-4 says replace the barrier and do not layer more on top; page 3-11 says redress over the soaked dressing and maintain pressure. The program's triage unit says replace it, but try not to remove the first layer and add another layer on top (T-12). All are shown. Instructor to reconcile.

reviewFlags.title: Tourniquet
reviewFlags.text: Tourniquet placement differs. FEMA 2019: as high as possible on the injured limb, closest to the torso (3-4). The program's triage unit says at least two inches above the wound, not over a joint, and to mark the time placed (T-12). Both shown. Instructor to reconcile.

reviewFlags.title: Recognize shock
reviewFlags.text: The program's triage unit adds: lay on back, elevate feet 6-10 inches, no food or drink (T-14), and lists "changes in skin color" as a shock sign (T-13). These are not in FEMA 2019 (3-5). Instructor to confirm.

reviewFlags.title: Open the airway
reviewFlags.text: Transcribed from a figure (image) in the manual. Verify against printed page 3-7.

reviewFlags.title: Open the airway
reviewFlags.text: The program's triage unit uses head-tilt/chin-lift (T-9) and, during triage, assigns Status: Black after two failed airway attempts without CPR (T-16, T-17). The FEMA chart here says to perform CPR if you know it (3-7). Context differs (one patient vs. mass casualty). Instructor to confirm.

reviewFlags.title: Stages of severe bleeding
reviewFlags.text: Table 3.1 gives Stage II blood loss as 15%-40%; the text on the same page says 15%-30%. Both are shown.

reviewFlags.title: Wound care & dressing
reviewFlags.text: The manual contradicts itself on blood-soaked dressings: page 3-4 says replace the barrier and do not layer more on top; page 3-11 says redress over the soaked dressing and maintain pressure. The program's triage unit says replace it, but try not to remove the first layer and add another layer on top (T-12). All are shown. Instructor to reconcile.
